title: A Self-Improving Coding Agent
data_curation: Not a focus of this paper. Evaluation data comprises a fixed random 50-question subset of SWE-Bench Verified and 50 random questions from LiveCodeBench, plus two synthetic benchmarks the agent itself curates: a file-editing benchmark built by cloning SWE-Bench repos, finding non-trivial consecutive-commit edits, and scoring how close the agent's edited file matches the target commit; and a codebase-navigation benchmark that asks the agent to locate the definition of an 'interesting' Python symbol given a reference. A second experiment adds AIME 2024 and GPQA Diamond. No training data is generated or filtered since SICA performs no weight updates.
curriculum: The 'curriculum' is the iterative self-improvement loop (Algorithm 1), not a pretrain->SFT->RL pipeline. SICA initializes a base agent A0, then for i=0..n-1 evaluates A_i on the benchmark set B, stores results in an archive, and selects the best-so-far agent A_i_hat (argmax utility) to act as the meta-agent that inspects the archive and edits the codebase to produce A_{i+1}. Within each meta-improvement iteration an archive_explorer sub-agent analyzes best/worst cases, reasoning sub-agents propose a feature, a software_developer implements and self-tests it, and a second developer independently verifies. The rationale is that coding-ability gains compound across iterations, and selecting the best agent as the next meta-agent (unlike fixed-meta-agent ADAS) lets improvements feed forward.
method: SICA (Self-Improving Coding Agent) is a non-gradient, self-referential agent that edits its own full Python codebase to improve utility. Unlike ADAS, which keeps a fixed meta-agent editing a single DSL forward function, SICA collapses meta- and target-agent: the best archive agent becomes the next meta-agent. Agent selection uses utility U = 0.5*p_score + 0.25*(1 - min(1, p_cost/$10)) + 0.25*(1 - min(1, p_time/300s)), with a 0.5 timeout penalty. The initial agent has file/shell/calculator/archive tools, coding/problem-solver/reasoning sub-agents, and an asynchronous LLM overseer (every 30s) that detects loops and can notify or cancel agents. Function calling uses XML tags as stop tokens. Models are Claude Sonnet 3.5 v2 for most agents and o3-mini for reasoning. Learned artifacts include a SmartEditor, AST/hybrid symbol locators, and context-summarization tools.
eval_metrics: Benchmarks: SWE-Bench Verified (50-question random subset), LiveCodeBench (50 questions), two self-curated synthetic benchmarks (file editing scored by content closeness; symbol navigation scored by locating path/to/file.py:line:col), plus AIME 2024 and GPQA Diamond. Metrics are benchmark accuracy plus per-problem dollar cost, wall-clock time, token count, and cache hit %, combined into the utility score. Headline: SWE-Bench Verified accuracy rose 17%->53% over 15 iterations (peak 0.53 at iter 14); file-editing 0.82->0.91; symbol navigation 0.35->0.40 (low due to data quality); LiveCodeBench ~0.65->0.71. AIME/GPQA showed little gain (o3-mini-high alone already scores 87%/79%; the agent system averaged 76%). The 15-iteration run cost about $7,000 in API spend.
key_results: SWE-Bench Verified (50-Q subset): 17%->53% accuracy over 15 self-improvement iterations; file-editing synthetic 0.82->0.91 and LiveCodeBench ~0.65->0.71, with per-problem cost ~$1.6-2.7 and total run cost ~$7,000; AIME/GPQA showed minimal gains.
evolution_note: SICA extends ADAS (2024) from a fixed-meta-agent/DSL setup to a truly self-referential agent editing its full Python codebase, reacting to hand-crafted orchestrators and prompt-optimization work (OPRO, Promptbreeder) and paralleling AlphaEvolve. By demonstrating scaffolding-only (non-weight) self-improvement, it motivates 2025+ work on jointly fine-tuning foundation-model weights with the agent system and on automated benchmark generation.
